metadata.note: ai-explainer / claude-hai. AI Debt Tracker WEEK 6. ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, answered), B09 (verdict artifact), B10 (handoff) and B11 (outro) only — every body beat illustrates its concept as a native animated Remotion scene (REBUILD LAW). The four source PNGs and their SVG sources are REFERENCE in pantry/, never slotted as media. The script's five body sections become eight body beats: 0:45 splits into the reader's mechanism (B02) and its score (B03), with the non-determinism the script mentions in one clause given its own beat (B04); 1:20 splits into the three-way check (B05) and where the gap actually sits (B06); 1:55 becomes B07; and the closing on-camera section becomes a limits beat. FIVE THINGS NOT TO GET WRONG: removing the borrowed ledger removes last week's recall advantage — agent start is LEVEL with B0, not ahead; precision moves the OTHER way and both halves belong on the frame; 93.3% against B0's 92.8% is LEVEL, never 'better'; the reader's 89.7%/98.8% are graded on 43 reports, not the 94 it read; and the week's gate records DELEGATED, not cleared. VERTICAL CUT: every beat re-renders from a <pattern>916 portrait composition — a re-layout, never a crop. The narration mp3s are copied from the 16:9 reel, not regenerated, so the two masters are the same edit.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about my A I debt tracker reading its own starting ledger from a company's last report, instead of borrowing it from the answer key, and measuring what that costs. This is week six of the A I Debt Tracker. It costs about eight points of recall — and that is the whole advantage I reported last week.

shot.visual_intent: COLD OPEN LAW: the ask is the week itself. It lands ANSWERED, and the answer says in its third line that this week undoes last week's headline. Nothing is held back for a reveal.

show.event: The ask types into the Claude composer.

show.at: on 'that is the whole advantage I reported last week'
show.event: The result lands ANSWERED with three output lines — the third is the cost.

props.segment: Reading the Opening Ledger Instead of Borrowing It
props.command: Stop handing the agent an opening ledger from the answer key. Make it read that ledger out of the company's own last report, run the same quarters again, and tell me exactly what the convenience was worth.
output: last week's merge fixes landed: wrong additions 26 → 3, precision 90.2% → 93.3% — level with doing nothing (92.8%), not better
the new opening-ledger reader finds 89.7% of the bonds and 98.8% of what it finds is right, against 83.8% for rules with no model
and reading its own start costs 7.9 points of recall — 97.9% → 90.1%, which puts it LEVEL with carrying last quarter forward (90.9%). Precision went the other way, up to 95.5%.

beats.narration_text: First, last week's leftovers. The tracker had added twenty-six bonds that weren't in the report. I fixed all three causes in the merge step, which is code, not a model. On the same readings, the wrong additions fell from twenty-six to three. Precision went from ninety to ninety-three percent — which is level with doing nothing, not better than it.

shot.visual_intent: Two bars on one shared unit — 6px per bond — so 3 against 26 is read as a length, not as two numbers. The three lines beneath are labelled as ACTIONS because 21+25+4 is what the merge step did, not the 26 broken down, and conflating them would be a real error.

show.at: on 'twenty-six bonds that weren't in the report'
show.event: The week 5 bar draws to full length.
The week 6 bar draws beneath it on the SAME scale — a stub.
Three actions land, each with its defect id.

props.verdict: Precision 90.2% → 93.3%. B0 is 92.8%, so that is level with B0, not better (+0.5 points against B0, -0.2 to +1.4). Recall held at 97.9%, still +7.0 points over B0.
props.note: The three that are left are not yet diagnosed. Loans are handled now too: a drawn amount counts as debt, a new commitment does not, and a repayment reduces it.

beats.narration_text: Now the crutch. Until this week, every quarter started from an opening ledger taken from the answer key — cheating a little, deliberately. So I built a reader for it. Code finds the tables that look like a debt note. The model points at the rows that are one bond. Code reads every number out of the cell.

shot.visual_intent: Same shape as the event reader from week 4, deliberately: code, then the model, then code. The model is the only accented card and the only one not labelled CODE, because the rule this whole project is built on is that it never types a number.

show.event: The old arrangement is named — oracle start.

show.at: on 'the model points at the rows'
show.event: The middle step lands in the accent, the only one that is not CODE.

show.at: on 'reads every number out of the cell'
show.event: The third step closes the sandwich.

props.sparkLine: Same rule as week one, a new job.

beats.narration_text: It read ninety-four opening reports. Graded on the forty-three the answer key covers, it found ninety percent of the bonds, and ninety-nine percent of what it found was right. Rules alone, with no model at all, found eighty-four percent. So the model buys recall, not precision — it finds rows the rules miss, and it isn't more accurate on them.

shot.visual_intent: Two metric pairs on one scale. The claim is about the SIZE of two gaps, so both gaps are drawn and the recall one is marked. The denominator split — 94 read, 43 graded — sits in the subtitle, because quoting 89.7% against 94 would be quoting it against the wrong set.

beats.narration_text: One more thing about that reader. Nine reports had to be asked again, because the first pass truncated the model's answers. Broadcom's January report gave thirty-six matching bonds the first time and twenty-two the second. Same report, same prompt, different answer. That variance is part of what this reader is, and I'm reporting it rather than averaging it away.

shot.visual_intent: Every other beat in this reel is a measurement. This one is the reason to distrust measurements of this kind: one input, two outputs, fourteen bonds apart. Drawn as two counts under a single bracket so the frame cannot be read as two different reports.

show.at: on 'thirty-six matching bonds the first time'
show.event: The first count lands.
The second lands beside it, visibly shorter, in the accent.
The two are bracketed as ONE report, not two.

props.why: The first pass stored only the first 3,000 characters of each model answer, so nine long answers could not be reused and were asked again.
props.meaning: The model's pointing is not the same from run to run. That variance is part of what the reader is, and it is reported rather than averaged away.
props.note: One run per report cannot say how often a swing like this happens.
props.source: SOURCE: AI Debt Tracker FRICTIONAL.md · docs/opening_reader.md · figdata.json

beats.narration_text: Then the real test. The same forty-five quarters, run three ways. Borrowing the start: ninety-eight percent recall. Reading its own start: ninety. That's a cost of about eight points. Precision went the other way, up to ninety-five and a half — fewer bonds held means fewer held wrongly. And here is the part that matters: against doing nothing, the agent is now level on recall.

shot.visual_intent: Six bars, one scale, three starts. The beat turns on the agent bar and the B0 bar ending at the same place on the recall rows while the accent bar runs PAST B0 on the precision rows. That is the week in one picture and it is drawn, not captioned.

The agent bar fills SHORT of it, in the accent.

beats.narration_text: The good news is that the gap is concentrated. Broadcom alone: twenty-three instruments found where the reports hold thirty-nine and forty. Snowflake and Super Micro, convertible tables the reader never found. And Core Scientific, whose opening reports were filed the same day as the report being predicted — so the point-in-time rule refuses them. That last one is the rule working.

shot.visual_intent: 'Most of it is a few companies' is a claim. Four named companies with the specific table each one hid is the same claim as evidence — and it separates the three misses from the one refusal, which is not a miss at all.

beats.narration_text: Last measurement: when an episode ends wrong, do the checks notice? Seventeen times out of fifty. They also flagged eleven of the thirty-six that ended right. So a third, with false alarms. And the investigators I added settled twenty-one of sixty-seven open questions — but changed no graded bond. Mostly they confirmed what the ledger already held.

shot.visual_intent: A rate drawn as a bar is a rectangle. Drawn as 50 countable cells with 17 filled, the thing you see is the 33 it missed — which is the honest subject of the beat. The investigators get a plain figure because their result is that nothing changed.

rows.limit: Everything here is on development quarters; the test split has not been touched. Every figure in this video is a development number.

The opening-ledger reader was graded against the same answer key that supplies the oracle start. It is being marked by the thing it is trying to replace. And it was graded on 43 of the 94 reports it read.
within 2% on 26 of 79 quarters at agent start, against 44 at oracle start. The bonds can be right while the total is not, and this is the weakest number in the video.

and no graded bond changed. All 24 maturity questions stayed open, because the passages the model pointed at gave no due date. 15 repayments are still unexplained. The investigators do not search older filings yet, which is where those answers are.

Which table rows are instruments, and which passage states a missing value, are qwen3:4b's judgments, flagged in every record. Every number in a ledger was parsed by code. The hand-check transcriptions are a model's reading, not a person's. The fresh hand-check agreed on 4 of 5 (P59). There was no fresh triage set this week, so all three triage sets are now calibrations.

props.gateNote: Handed to Claude end to end before the week started. The one decision taken during it was to resume the runs after the laptop ran low on memory. No person has reviewed the transcriptions or the results — for weeks 3 to 6. (Not measured in figdata.json — recorded in manifests/week6_gate.json.)
next: then version 1: freeze, scale up, run the whole development window unattended
props.source: SOURCE: narration_script.md notes · FRICTIONAL.md · docs/agent_start.md · docs/opening_reader.md · figdata.json

beats.narration_text: So: the merge fixes cut the wrong additions from twenty-six to three, and a new reader builds the opening ledger out of the company's last report — ninety percent of the bonds, ninety-nine percent of those right. Standing on its own reading, the tracker loses about eight points of recall and is level with doing nothing. It gains on precision. The checks notice a third of its mistakes, and nobody has reviewed any of it.

shot.visual_intent: Judgment beat. The artifact page is the point (ILLUSTRATE LAW carve-out). The third finding is the one that undoes last week's headline, and it is in the middle rather than buried at the end.

show.event: Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause.

props.artifactTitle: Reading the Opening Ledger Instead of Borrowing It
props.artifactHeading: What week 6 built, and what it is allowed to claim
artifactLines: Three merge fixes, all code: launch notices fold into the priced bond (P57), a bond named with no amount becomes a question (P56), the banks' option is recorded but not added (P58). On the same readings the wrong additions fell 26 → 3 and precision rose 90.2% → 93.3% — level with B0's 92.8%, not better.

An opening-ledger reader on the same rule as the event reader: code finds the debt tables, qwen3:4b points at the rows that are one instrument, code reads every value from the cited cell. 94 reports read; graded on 43, recall 89.7% and precision 98.8%, against 83.8% / 97.9% for rules with no model. The model adds recall, not precision.

THE WEEK'S CHECK (A4). Same 45 quarters, borrowed start against read start: recall 97.9% → 90.1%, a cost of -7.9 points of recall, paired, -2.0 to -15.3. Precision moved the other way, 93.3% → 95.5%. Against B0 the agent is now LEVEL on recall (90.9%) and ahead on precision (92.8%). Last week's +7.0 points over doing nothing was the borrowed ledger.

The gap is concentrated: Broadcom alone accounts for much of it, Snowflake and Super Micro hid their convertible tables, and Core Scientific's opening reports are refused by the point-in-time rule (P60) — the rule working, counted in the gap rather than worked around. The reader is also not deterministic: Broadcom's January 2025 report gave 36 bonds on one ask and 22 on the next.

Of the 50 quarters that ended wrong, the checks flagged 17; they flagged 11 of 36 that ended right. Investigators settled 21 of 67 questions and changed no graded bond. Total debt is within 2% on 26 of 79 quarters, down from 44. The gate records the week DELEGATED, not CLEARED.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Find the place where your evaluation hands your system something it would have to work out for itself in the real thing — a label, a starting state, a cleaned-up input. Take it away and re-run. Whatever you lose is a number you were never really measuring.

shot.visual_intent: HANDOFF LAW: a real prompt, read ALOUD and then discussed. One of exactly two typing beats. It is this week's finding — that a convenience inside an evaluation is an unmeasured claim — turned into something a viewer can run on their own work.

show.event: The prompt types into the composer.

props.command: Find every place my evaluation hands the system something it would have to produce for itself in production — a gold label, a starting state, a cleaned input, a retrieved document. List them, pick the one doing the most work, make the system generate it instead, and re-run the same evaluation unchanged. Report both numbers side by side and tell me what that convenience was worth.
